title: Post Sample Aberrations in STEM
content: Recent developments in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), particularly the uptake of new direct electron detectors, are generating interest in all forms of 4D STEM, where an electron scattering pattern is recorded for each probe position. One of the key advantages of this type of imaging mode is that it can be very much more efficient than conventional bright field (BF) or high-angle annular dark field STEM (HAADF) [1,2]. BF STEM traditionally relies on a small detector to ensure a large coherence envelope, collecting only a fraction of the transmitted electrons, while HAADF STEM similarly collects only that small number of electrons that are scattered to high angles. On the other hand, pixelated detectors are, at least in principle, able to make use of almost every transmitted electron, reducing the dose required to form an image. One way of making use of every electron is to use a simple reconstruction, where the shifts induced by aberrations [3] are corrected in post-processing, to allow a BF image with more pixels than the number of probe positions and a better signal to noise ratio than the image formed by a single pixel [4-6] (Figure 1).
